Field surveys of White-dotted skate (Bathyraja albomaculata) in the southwestern Atlantic have provided detailed insights into its reproductive biology and growth patterns. Analysis of a large specimen series indicates that neonates emerge from their egg cases with a total length of approximately 17.8 cm [Lb = approximately 17.8 cm], a size consistent with the 0.18 ratio of the asymptotic length observed across the Bathyraja genus. Under the persistent thermal conditions of the Patagonian shelf, where bottom water temperatures average 5.7 °C [T = 5.7 °C], the incubation period within the egg case spans roughly 671 days [ab = roughly 671 days] based on embryonic growth rates calculated for related species. This exceptionally protracted development is among the longest recorded for any rajiform, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by cold-water metabolism. Upon hatching, young skates are fully formed miniatures of the adults and begin an extended period of slow somatic growth that will ultimately allow them to reach considerable body sizes.

As individuals progress through their juvenile and sub-adult stages, they undergo a gradual increase in body dimensions over many years. Available growth data suggest that the ultimate total length attained by this species is approximately 99 cm [Li = approximately 99 cm], representing the asymptotic body size derived from length-at-age relationships. Reaching this maximum dimension requires an extended period of sustained feeding and favorable environmental conditions, as growth rates for cold-water elasmobranchs are characteristically low. The species is not among the largest of the arhynchobatid skates, but a 99 cm maximum does place it in the upper size range for its genus in the region. The relationship between length and mass in Bathyraja albomaculata follows a typical power function for skates; consequently, an individual achieving the asymptotic length would have a corresponding ultimate wet weight of roughly 8.6 kilograms [Wwi = roughly 8.6 kilograms]. This substantial body mass supports the energetic requirements of a benthic foraging lifestyle centered on crustaceans and small fishes.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this skate is tied closely to body size rather than strictly to chronological age. Analysis of clasper calcification and gonadal development in males indicates that puberty is typically attained at a total length of approximately 65 cm [Lp = approximately 65 cm]. Reaching this threshold necessitates roughly a decade of growth, as inferred from vertebral banding patterns and size-at-age models for the species. This length at puberty represents roughly two-thirds of the ultimate length, a proportion that aligns with the general pattern observed in other slow-growing batoids. Once an individual surpasses this size, the reproductive system becomes fully functional, enabling participation in the annual breeding aggregations that occur on the outer continental shelf. The timing of this maturation event is critical for population dynamics, as it introduces a significant delay before individuals can contribute to the next generation.

Reproductive output in the White-dotted skate, constrained by the cold waters of its habitat, is relatively modest compared to teleost fishes. In the typical thermal environment of 5.7 °C [T = 5.7 °C], females deposit a single pair of fertilised egg cases per reproductive event [N_R_i = single pair of fertilised egg cases per reproductive event], with a maximum frequency of approximately 6.5 laying events each year [F_R_i = approximately 6.5 laying events each year]. This reproductive rate is derived from the species' position on the slow end of the life-history continuum, where energy is allocated preferentially toward somatic maintenance rather than high fecundity. The egg cases are deposited on soft sediment habitats, where they undergo the lengthy incubation period described earlier. Each capsule is tough and durable, providing physical protection to the yolk-dependent embryo throughout its 22-month development. This combination of low fecundity and extended embryonic development makes the species particularly vulnerable to fisheries-related mortality.

Longevity estimates for Bathyraja albomaculata, derived from tag-recapture studies and analysis of growth increments in vertebral centra, place the maximum lifespan at approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] under the ambient thermal regime of 5.7 °C [T = 5.7 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of deepwater and high-latitude skate species, which offset slow growth and low reproductive output with a prolonged adult phase that allows multiple breeding seasons over a lifetime. An individual that matures at roughly 65 cm and lives to 17 years likely participates in numerous reproductive cycles, gradually contributing to population replacement. Senescence in this species is poorly documented, but the oldest individuals captured in trawl surveys exhibit worn dentition and reduced body condition, suggesting a gradual physiological decline. The combination of a late age at maturity, extended egg case incubation, and low fecundity underscores the inherently low rebound potential of this skate, making it highly sensitive to increases in fishing pressure.
